The key insight for the 2x ADR is that EC2 horizontal scaling and the Redis Socket.io adapter are not separate decisions - they must be deployed together because horizontal scaling creates the problem the adapter solves
Kubernetes at 2-3 instances with a 3-person team (2 junior) adds significant operational overhead that isn't yet justified - the ADR should explicitly state team capability as a constraint

lessons.title: Phase 6: Engineering Retrospective And Forward Plan
lessons.lessonGoal: Produce the senior engineering retrospective that closes the CollabFlow engagement: a complete architectural state document, a retrospective on what worked and what didn't, and a forward engineering plan grounded in the current production evidence.

sections.title: The Retrospective As The Most Important Engineering Document After The Assessment
sections.content: A senior engineer's final deliverable is not the code — it's the documentation that makes the code intelligible and improvable to everyone who comes after. THE ENGINEERING RETROSPECTIVE is the document that closes a significant engagement: it captures the current architectural state with full ADR lineage, reflects honestly on what worked and what didn't, and provides a forward engineering plan with specific evidence grounding each recommendation. This document is not an exercise in self-promotion; it is the transfer of institutional knowledge from the engineer who did the work to the team that will continue it. An engineering retrospective that describes a system accurately is worth more to that team than any amount of excellent code documentation.

sections.title: A Ship's Log At The End Of A Voyage: Complete Record, Honest Account, Next Voyage Plan
sections.content: A ship's log at the end of a long voyage serves three purposes: it records exactly where the ship went and what conditions it encountered (the architectural state and decisions made); it records what worked and what didn't (the honest retrospective); and it provides guidance for the next voyage (the forward plan). A ship's log that omits the difficult moments, the decisions that were revised, or the failed approaches gives the next captain a false picture that will cause them to repeat avoidable mistakes. This retrospective's value is directly proportional to its honesty: the things that didn't work as planned are as important to document as the successes, because they're the decisions that someone will be tempted to revisit.

sections.title: The Three Components Of The Engineering Retrospective
sections.content:
COMPONENT 1: ARCHITECTURAL STATE DOCUMENT
- Current architecture diagram (what it looks like today)
- ADR index (all 7 ADRs with status and brief summary)
- Known technical debt (what was deferred and why)
- Current SLO status (are we meeting the targets we set?)

COMPONENT 2: RETROSPECTIVE (what worked, what didn't)
- What worked:
  * Observability first (enabled all subsequent evidence-based decisions)
  * Feature flag containment (Incident 1 resolved in 9 minutes)
  * Evidence-first approach (BullMQ justified by event loop lag data)
  * Weekly metrics review (caught memory leak 22 days before OOM)
- What didn't work as planned:
  * Redis maxmemory not reviewed during BullMQ deployment (Incident 1)
  * Phase 3 read replica deferral was correct, but the 3-query activity
    endpoint fix revealed that code review wasn't catching N+1 patterns
  * Socket.io memory leak shipped because disconnect lifecycle wasn't
    in the code review checklist

COMPONENT 3: FORWARD ENGINEERING PLAN
- Immediate (Month 6): 2x horizontal scaling + Redis adapter
- Short term (Month 7-8): 4x load test, read replica decision
- Medium term (Month 9-12): Kubernetes evaluation at 5x,
  multi-region evaluation if geographic expansion is planned
- Process improvements: deployment checklist additions (Redis capacity,
  Socket.io lifecycle), code review checklist additions (N+1 patterns)

sections.title: Why The 'What Didn't Work' Section Is The Most Professionally Valuable
sections.content: This is the single most important, most professionally challenging discipline of the retrospective: the honest accounting of what didn't work as planned. Most engineers writing retrospectives overweight the successes and underweight the failures, producing a document that reads well but helps future engineers poorly. The two things that went wrong in this engagement — Redis maxmemory not reviewed during BullMQ deployment (creating Incident 1) and the Socket.io disconnect lifecycle not in the code review checklist (creating the memory leak) — are MORE valuable to document than the six things that went right, because they reveal the SYSTEMIC GAPS that the current process has. A future engineer reading this retrospective and seeing 'we deployed BullMQ without reviewing Redis capacity requirements, which caused Incident 1' will add Redis capacity to their deployment checklist. A future engineer who only reads about the successes will repeat the same mistake.

sections.title: The Complete Engineering Retrospective For CollabFlow Month 5
sections.content: This demonstrates the complete retrospective document, including the honest accounting of failures that makes it genuinely useful:
sections.code:
# COLLABFLOW ENGINEERING RETROSPECTIVE
# Month 5 | Senior Engineer Review

## ARCHITECTURAL STATE

### Current Architecture (Month 5)
- Backend: Node.js/Express, EC2 c5.xlarge (4 CPU/8GB), 1 instance
- Database: PostgreSQL 14, RDS db.t3.medium (separate from app)
  (migrated from same-instance to RDS in Month 3 for Phase 3 work)
- Redis: Elasticache r6g.medium (512MB), maxmemory configured
- BullMQ: Email notification queue, 3 attempts, exponential backoff
- Observability: Prometheus + Grafana (4 golden signals), pino logs,
  OpenTelemetry traces (Jaeger)
- CI/CD: GitHub Actions, blue-green deploy to EC2
- Auth: JWT (15-min access) + DB-stored rotating refresh tokens

### ADR Index
| ADR | Title | Status |
|-----|-------|--------|
| 001 | JWT refresh token rotation | Accepted |
| 002 | Secrets to AWS Secrets Manager | Accepted |
| 003 | Four golden signal instrumentation | Accepted |
| 004 | GitHub Actions CI/CD | Accepted |
| 005 | BullMQ for email queue | Accepted |
| 006 | EC2 autoscaling + Redis Socket.io | Pending (Month 6) |
| 007 | Redis Pub/Sub for Socket.io | Pending (Month 6) |

### Known Technical Debt
- No pgBouncer (will be needed at 5+ instances, Month 9-10)
- Socket.io Redis adapter not yet deployed (Month 6)
- Kubernetes not yet evaluated (deferred to 5x scale, Month 9+)
- Email idempotency keys stored in BullMQ job data; should
  be persisted to DB for cross-restart idempotency

## RETROSPECTIVE

### What Worked Well
1. Observability first principle: every evidence-based decision
   in Phases 3-5 was made with real production data rather than
   projections. The BullMQ decision, in particular, was directly
   justified by the 380ms event loop lag measurement.

2. Feature flag containment: Incident 1 was resolved in 9 minutes
   with minimal user impact specifically because the feature flag
   to disable email queueing was already implemented as part of
   the BullMQ deployment. Users sent messages throughout.

3. Weekly metrics review: caught the Socket.io memory leak 22 days
   before it would have caused an OOM crash. The value of this
   practice, established early, exceeded expectations.

4. Evidence-based 'not yet' decisions: deferring read replicas,
   Kubernetes, and Redis Pub/Sub until warranted saved significant
   engineering capacity for the security and observability work
   that genuinely mattered at current scale.

### What Didn't Work As Planned
1. Redis capacity not reviewed during BullMQ deployment:
   ADR-005 documented the BullMQ decision but did not include
   a Redis capacity review step. Incident 1 resulted directly
   from this gap. Action: Redis capacity step added to infra
   deployment checklist.

2. N+1 query pattern slipped through code review:
   The activity endpoint's N+1 pattern (50 user queries per request)
   shipped to production and ran for 6 weeks before being caught
   in the Phase 3 query optimization work. Code review checklist
   now includes N+1 pattern check.

3. Socket.io disconnect lifecycle not in review checklist:
   The memory leak shipped because disconnect handlers are a
   non-obvious Socket.io resource lifecycle requirement that
   wasn't part of the review process for new event handlers.
   Engineering wiki now documents Socket.io lifecycle patterns.

## FORWARD ENGINEERING PLAN

### Month 6 (Immediate)
- 2x horizontal scaling: EC2 autoscaling group (2 instances) + ALB
- Redis Pub/Sub adapter for Socket.io (deployed simultaneously)
- ADR-006 and ADR-007 implemented

### Month 7-8 (Short Term)
- Load test at 4x (480 concurrent) with k6
- EXPLAIN analysis of DB under 4x load
- Decision on read replicas based on load test evidence
- pgBouncer evaluation (based on connection count at 3 instances)

### Month 9-12 (Medium Term)
- Kubernetes evaluation (justified if operational complexity of
  managing 5+ EC2 instances exceeds Kubernetes learning cost)
- Multi-region evaluation (driven by geographic user distribution,
  not projected; requires data on where users are)
- Email idempotency persistence to DB (current BullMQ-only approach
  loses idempotency keys on Redis restart)

### Process Improvements (Ongoing)
- Monthly SLO review: all three SLOs currently met
- Pre-deploy checklist: Redis capacity, connection pool math
- Code review checklist: N+1 patterns, Socket.io lifecycle
- Weekly metrics review: continuing as established practice
sections.explanation: This retrospective demonstrates all three components: the architectural state document provides a complete picture of what the system looks like now and why (ADR index); the honest retrospective gives the most value by documenting the failures alongside successes with specific action items for each; and the forward plan is sequenced and evidence-based, deferring decisions that require load test evidence rather than asserting them as projections. The 'What Didn't Work' section is specifically the most professionally valuable part — the three failures documented here will prevent similar failures for every engineer who reads this document.

sections.title: The Engineering Retrospective As The Primary Artifact Of Senior Engineering Engagement
sections.content: Real engineering organizations evaluate the quality of a senior engineer's engagement primarily by the artifacts they leave behind, not by the code they wrote. Code can be rewritten; the reasoning behind architectural decisions is often irretrievable without documentation. A well-written engineering retrospective is the artifact that converts the knowledge accumulated during an engagement into institutional memory that benefits the team for years. Real engineering leaders specifically look for the honesty and specificity of the 'what didn't work' section: an engineer who documents their mistakes honestly and converts them into systemic process improvements has demonstrated the most valuable senior engineering quality — the ability to make the system better not just by their own work but by improving how the team works.

sections.title: Common Engineering Retrospective Mistakes
sections.content:
1. Omitting or minimizing the 'what didn't work' section, producing a document that reads as self-promotional rather than genuinely useful to future engineers.

2. Not connecting the 'what didn't work' items to specific, implemented process changes, leaving the failures documented but not addressed.

3. Expressing the forward engineering plan as firm commitments rather than evidence-based decisions contingent on specific measurements, creating expectations that can't be met when the evidence eventually arrives.

4. Not updating the ADR index to include ADRs still pending (Month 6's horizontal scaling ADRs), giving future engineers an incomplete picture of decisions in flight.

5. Writing the retrospective for an audience that already knows the system rather than for the engineer who will join in month 9 and needs to understand why the architecture is the way it is.

sections.title: The Retrospective As The Final Expression Of This Curriculum's Core Discipline
sections.content: This retrospective is the final expression of the single discipline that this curriculum has built across all three levels: evidence-first, evidence-grounded, evidence-documented engineering. Every decision in this retrospective — from 'observability first' in Month 1 to 'Redis Pub/Sub deferred until horizontal scaling warranted it' in Month 5 — is traceable to specific evidence. The ADR index makes every decision and its evidence findable. The retrospective's honest 'what didn't work' section makes the evidence of failures available too. The forward plan's 'pending load test evidence' notes make clear which future decisions still await their evidence. This is not perfectionism or over-documentation; it is the minimal documentation that makes engineering decisions durable, transferable, and improvable by anyone who works on this system after you.

sections.title: Auditing Your Own Retrospective For The Properties That Make It Genuinely Useful
sections.content: The self-audit for a retrospective's usefulness: read it as the engineer who joins the team in Month 9 with no prior context. Can they determine what the system looks like today? (Architectural state document.) Can they determine why the specific architectural choices were made rather than alternatives? (ADR index.) Can they determine what process improvements have been made in response to what failures? (What Didn't Work with action items.) Can they determine what decisions are still pending and what evidence will drive them? (Forward plan.) If any of these questions cannot be answered by reading the retrospective, the document has a gap. Fix the gap before finalizing.

checkpoints.question: Why is the 'What Didn't Work' section described as the most professionally valuable part of the retrospective?
options: Failures should be emphasized more than successes in all engineering documentation

The failures reveal the systemic gaps in the current process that will cause future engineers to repeat the same mistakes if not documented. Documenting 'we deployed BullMQ without Redis capacity review, causing Incident 1' and the action taken (added to deployment checklist) transfers learning from a specific incident to a systemic improvement that benefits every future deployment
Engineering retrospectives should always be self-critical to demonstrate humility
The 'What Worked' section should be omitted to make retrospectives more efficient
checkpoints.explanation: Failures reveal systemic gaps that future engineers will repeat without documentation. Converting specific incidents into systemic process improvements is the highest-value content in a retrospective.

checkpoints.question: The forward plan says 'read replica decision based on load test evidence at 4x.' An engineer asks: 'Why not just decide now that we'll need a read replica at 4x?' What is the correct answer?
options: Read replicas are always needed at 4x scale regardless of workload

The load test at 4x will reveal whether the DB bottleneck is genuine read throughput (requiring a read replica) or a specific unindexed query (requiring a free index fix). Deciding now commits to a specific, expensive infrastructure before knowing which of these it actually is. The evidence-first principle: the load test IS the evidence that makes the correct decision
Load tests are always done for ceremonial reasons and their results don't affect decisions
It is impossible to plan architecture decisions in advance
checkpoints.explanation: The 4x load test provides the evidence that distinguishes a query-level fix (free) from a read replica (expensive infrastructure). Deciding now would commit to one without knowing which is actually needed.

checkpoints.question: What is the final, most important property a senior engineering retrospective must have?
options: It must be as long as possible to demonstrate thoroughness

It must be written for the engineer who joins in month 9 with no prior context: they should be able to determine what the system looks like, why each architectural choice was made, what failed and what changed as a result, and what decisions are still pending and what evidence will drive them
It must emphasize the senior engineer's personal contributions
It must include a complete code review of all changes made during the engagement
checkpoints.explanation: The retrospective's audience is the future engineer with no prior context - every section must serve that reader's need to understand the current state, the reasoning behind it, the failures and their process responses, and the pending decisions.
